6.01.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "which hip device is this?"
- "Parallel screws, no plate → **cannulated screws**; one bolt + small plate with a locking screw → **FNS** (femoral neck system)."
- "Big lag screw sliding in the **barrel** of a side plate → **DHS** (dynamic hip screw), 135°; same parts at **95°** → **DCS** (dynamic condylar screw)."
- "Solid **U-shaped blade** forged to the plate → **angled blade plate**; nail in the canal + screw or blade into the head → **cephalomedullary nail**."

### The one feature that tells each apart
| Device | Look for | Angle | Slides? | Where it goes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cannulated screws | 3 parallel partially threaded screws ± washers | along the neck | yes, along the screws | femoral neck |
| FNS | 1 bolt + 1 antirotation screw through a short plate | 130° | yes, bolt in the plate barrel | femoral neck, vertical (Pauwels III) |
| DHS | lag screw + barrel + side plate | 130–150° | yes | stable trochanteric, basicervical |
| DCS | same parts, longer plate | 95° | used as fixed angle | subtrochanteric, distal femur |
| Angled blade plate | blade and plate **one piece**, no barrel | 95° or 130° | no | subtroch, osteotomy, nonunion |
| Cephalomedullary nail | nail in canal + screw(s) or blade into the head | 125–130° | yes | unstable trochanteric, reverse oblique, subtroch |
| Proximal femoral locking plate | spoon-shaped head, holes **in one line** | multiple locked | no | rare: comminution, portal destroyed |

- **Subtroch → five options** → blade plate · DCS · locking plate · PFNA (proximal femoral nail antirotation) · standard nail (AO)

- Five subtrochanteric fixation options (AO)
- Blade, condylar and proximal femur locked plates, photo (Nagah)
- DHS and DCS side by side, angles and TAD (Handbook)

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Neck → screws / FNS · stable trochanter → DHS · unstable trochanter → nail · subtroch → long nail (95° plate if not) · revision → blade**

### Two families, two mechanics
- **Extramedullary** (DHS, DCS, blade, locking plate) → plate on the lateral cortex → long lever arm → load-bearing
- **Intramedullary** (PFN = proximal femoral nail, PFNA, Gamma, InterTAN, recon) → nail near the load axis → shorter lever arm → load-sharing (Campbell)
- The nail also blocks lateral escape of the head fragment → stops **medialisation** of the shaft (AO)

- Unstable trochanteric fracture fixed with PFNA (AO)

6.02.b:
### Cannulated screws — card

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "cannulated screws"
- "**Cannulated cancellous screws**, 6.5–7.3 mm, **partially threaded**, put over guide wires, usually three in an **inverted triangle**."
- "They act as **lag screws** → compression across the neck fracture, then **controlled sliding** as it settles; for **undisplaced** fractures and **displaced ones in the young**."

#### Recognise it · parts
- Hollow screw over a guide wire · partial thread · washer where space permits → lag effect → ch 4
- Size **6.5, 7.0 or 7.3 mm** (Campbell) · thread length often **16 mm**, so every thread sits in the head (AO)

- Inverted triangle and diamond configurations (Campbell)
- Cannulated screws on guide wires (Prof Abdel Karim)

#### How it works — why the inverted triangle
| Rule | Why |
|---|---|
| Screws **parallel** | head slides and impacts; threads must not cross the fracture (AO) |
| **Inferior screw on the calcar** | resists varus (Campbell) |
| **Two superior screws** | anterior and posterior cortical support (Campbell) |
| Screws **peripheral**, not central | buttress in every direction (AO) |

- Three parallel 7.3 mm screws with cross-section (AO)

PITFALL — "two superior screws carry the tension"?
- Handbook and Nagah → the superior side is the tension side, so two screws go there
- Campbell / AO → the point is **cortical support**: inferior on the calcar, the others against the anterior and posterior cortex
- Say → "**inferior on the calcar, two above against the cortices, all parallel and peripheral**"

#### Indications · contraindications
- Undisplaced or valgus-impacted neck fracture → fix it to prevent displacement · displaced in the young → anatomical reduction, often open, then screws (AO)
- **Not** for basicervical or vertical fractures → fixed angle: **DHS + derotation screw** or FNS (Miller) · elderly displaced → arthroplasty → ch 10

#### Insertion — instruments in order
1) Fracture table, closed reduction, AP and lateral check; open reduction if not anatomical
2) Stab incision, split vastus lateralis; start **above the lesser trochanter** (Miller)
3) **Inferocentral guide wire first**, on the calcar, screw <4 mm from it (Campbell)
4) **Parallel guide** → posterosuperior then anterosuperior wires, ≥1 cm apart (Campbell)
5) Depth gauge → screw = wire length **minus 5 mm** (Campbell)
6) Self-drilling self-tapping screws + washers → release traction → tighten repeatedly (AO)

- Tightening order → anterosuperior → inferior → **posterosuperior last** (Handbook) · posterior comminution → a **fourth screw** (diamond), which may sit outside bone posteriorly (Campbell)

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Calcar wire first · posterosuperior screw tightened last**

#### What goes wrong
- **Subtrochanteric fracture** → entry below the lesser trochanter or several drill holes = stress riser (Campbell)
- **Posterosuperior screw** → perforates the neck where the retinacular vessels enter → AVN (avascular necrosis) (Harborview)
- Neck **shortening** >1 cm → 42% of Garden I, 63% of Garden II (Campbell) · **varus** malreduction → failure (Miller)

- Posterosuperior quadrant of the neck to avoid (Harborview)

### FNS (Femoral Neck System) — card

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "FNS"
- "**Femoral Neck System**: a **bolt** and an **antirotation screw** through a short **lateral plate** held by one **locking screw**."
- "**Fixed-angle sliding** device → angular and rotational stability like a DHS, small incision like screws; for neck fractures in **younger** patients, esp. Pauwels III."

- Recognise it → **one barrel, two elements**, very short plate · bolt **10 mm**, 70–130 mm, tip ≈5 mm from subchondral bone (Jin 2025)
- Antirotation screw = bolt length, through the bolt's aperture · locking screw in the distal plate hole · inserted with a **130° guide** (Jin 2025)
- Antirotation screw **6.4 mm** at **7.5°** to the bolt → tips spread in the head · locking screw **5.0 mm** (Teng 2022)
- Built-in **20 mm** of sliding compression (He 2021) · other fixed-angle neck devices → Targon FN, CONQUEST FN (Campbell)

- Three fixed-angle neck devices (Campbell)
- High Pauwels femoral neck fracture fixed with FNS, AP X-ray (Campbell)

EXAM PEARL — young neck: screws or fixed angle?
- FNS versus screws → less AVN, shortening and fluoroscopy (Campbell)
- Pauwels III → **more nonunion with cannulated screws** than with fixed-angle devices (Campbell)
- **FAITH trial**, age >50 → screws vs sliding hip screw: **same reoperation** · AVN 9% vs 5% (Campbell)

6.03.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "DHS"
- "**Dynamic hip screw**: a **lag screw** sliding in the **barrel** of a **side plate** fixed to the shaft by cortical screws; standard **135°**."
- "On weight bearing the screw **slides** → **controlled impaction = dynamic compression**; key → **centre–centre**, **TAD** (tip–apex distance) **<25 mm**."
- "For **stable trochanteric (31A1)** and **basicervical** fractures; **not** for reverse oblique, subtrochanteric extension or a broken lateral wall."

### Recognise it
- **Barrel + side plate** in one piece, a separate **fat lag screw**, a small **compression screw** at the back
- Versus blade plate → **round barrel, separate screw** · versus DCS → **135°**, not 95°

- Sliding hip screw parts, photo (Rockwood)

### Parts & sizes
| Part | Exam numbers |
|---|---|
| Lag screw | thread **12.5 mm** (Rockwood) · thread length **22 mm** (Nagah) · 65–130 mm long (Rockwood) |
| Barrel | standard **38 mm** (Handbook) · **keyed** → no rotation of the screw (Rockwood) |
| Plate angle | **130–150°**, 135° standard (Handbook) |
| Side plate | **2–4 holes** usual (Rockwood) |
| Cortical screws | **4.5 mm**, bicortical (Rockwood) |
| Compression screw | into the back of the lag screw |
| Coupling screws | long → removal · short → inserting the lag screw into the plate (Nagah) |

EXAM PEARL — short vs standard barrel (Nagah)
- Thread 22 mm + sliding 20 mm + standard barrel 38 mm = **80 mm**
- Lag screw ≤80 mm → **short barrel**, to keep room to slide · usual choice → standard barrel

### How it works
- Lag screw slides along the barrel axis → impaction → compression, **only if** central in the head (AO)
- Compression comes from **releasing traction**, the **compression screw**, then **weight bearing** (Nagah)

- DHS, 2-hole plate, two-part trochanteric fracture, TAD drawn (AO)

PITFALL — "the compression screw makes the DHS static"?
- Nagah → the compression screw turns the DHS from dynamic to static
- Rockwood → sliding continues, up to 5 mm expected, so the compression screw must not be left proud
- Say → "**it compresses on the table and stops disengagement; it does not stop sliding**"

### Indications · contraindications
| Use it | Avoid it |
|---|---|
| **Stable trochanteric** (31A1, old A2.1) (Handbook) | **Reverse oblique** (31A3) → shaft medialises (Rockwood) |
| **Basicervical** + derotation screw (Miller) | **Subtrochanteric extension** (Miller) |
| Neck fracture, alternative to screws (AO) | **Incompetent lateral wall** (Miller) |
| Young osteotomy patients | Posteromedial comminution (Handbook) |

- **Lateral wall thickness** → measured 3 cm below the innominate tubercle, on a 135° line to the fracture (Campbell)

PITFALL — lateral wall thickness cut-off
- Handbook → DHS contraindicated if the lateral wall is **<20.5 mm**
- Campbell → **<21 mm** predicts lateral wall fracture, 95% sensitivity
- Say → "**about 20 mm: thinner → nail, or DHS + trochanteric stabilising plate (TSP)**"

### Insertion — instruments in order
1) **Fracture table** → traction, internal rotation, adduction; lift any posterior sag (Handbook)
2) Lateral incision from the **vastus ridge** distally → fascia lata → elevate vastus lateralis, coagulate perforators (Campbell)
3) **135° angle guide** at the level of the lesser trochanter → **guide wire** centre–centre (Rockwood)
4) Wire to ≈5 mm from the joint → **direct measuring device** (Campbell)
5) **Triple reamer** set 5 mm short → screw track + barrel + barrel–plate junction (Handbook)
6) **Tap** in dense young bone (Campbell)
7) **Lag screw** on the **insertion wrench**; final handle **parallel to the shaft** → barrel mates (Handbook)
8) Plate over the screw → **impactor** → flush with bone (Campbell)
9) Plate clamp → **4.5 mm cortical screws** → release traction → **compression screw** (Rockwood)

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Wire → measure → ream → tap → screw → plate → impact → screws → compress**

- Lag screw tip 5–10 mm from subchondral bone · 5 mm shorter than reamed if collapse is expected · ± provisional antirotation wire (Rockwood)
- Fine depth → **half a turn (180°) ≈ 1.5 mm** of advance (Campbell)

- Sliding hip screw insertion, step by step (Campbell)
- Antirotation wire, lag screw near subchondral bone, 135° two-hole plate (Rockwood)

CLINICAL PEARL — the "hairline crack" reduction
- Best defence against collapse → **anteromedial cortex reduced** to a hairline crack on the AP view (Rockwood)
- Say → "I reduce the medial cortex first; the implant only holds what I reduced"

CLINICAL PEARL — problems in theatre
- **Posterior sag** → seen on the **lateral** view → lift the shaft with a Hohmann (Nagah)
- **Guide wire comes out with the reamer** → reinsert it through a centring sleeve, or a reversed lag screw in the track (Nagah)
- Prevent it → screw and reamer a few mm **shorter than the wire** (Handbook)
- **Plate not flush** → wrong angle; forcing it gaps the medial cortex (Rockwood)

### How many screws in the side plate?
- **Two-hole plate** enough for stable fractures (Miller) · **four holes** for unstable or osteoporotic bone (Rockwood) · Nagah → same ("two make it stable, we use four")

### Add-ons
| Add-on | What it does | When |
|---|---|---|
| **Antirotation (derotation) screw** | cancellous screw **cranial** to the lag screw → rotational control (AO) | basicervical, neck, posterior comminution |
| **TSP** | mounted on the DHS plate → buttresses the greater trochanter and lateral wall (Handbook) | thin or broken lateral wall, greater trochanter (GT) fragment |
| **Locking DHS plate** | locking holes in the side plate | TSP does not fit it (Handbook) |

- DHS with a parallel derotation screw for a neck fracture (Campbell)
- Trochanteric stabilising plate mounted on the DHS side plate (Campbell)
- Measuring lateral wall thickness (Campbell)

### What goes wrong
- **Cut-out** → 6.10 · **excessive collapse** → shortening, **medialisation**, weak abductors (Miller)
- **Iatrogenic lateral wall fracture** while reaming for the barrel → ≈15% with DHS (Rockwood)
- **Prominent compression screw** after sliding → lateral thigh pain (Rockwood)

- Healed fracture: shortening, backed-out antirotation screw, prominent compression screw (Rockwood)

EXAM PEARL — removing a DHS (Nagah)
- Long **coupling screw** into the lag screw → unscrew
- Screw will not come out → turn it **two turns in** to free it, then unscrew

6.04.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "DCS"
- "**Dynamic condylar screw**: the same lag screw and barrel as a DHS but at **95°** → a **fixed-angle** device."
- "For the **distal femur** and the **subtrochanteric** region; easier than a blade plate → correct in **two planes**, not three."

### Recognise it · parts
- Lag screw + **95° barrel–plate**; longer plate; condylar end shaped for the lateral condyle
- Proximal → guide wire **2 cm proximal to the vastus ridge**, at 95° to the shaft (MIPO)
- Distal → needs **≥4 cm** of intact condyle above the notch (Campbell) · entry ≈2 cm from the joint (Nagah)

- Dynamic condylar screw on the distal femur (AO)

### How it works
- Fixed angle → holds a short metaphyseal block against varus (AO)
- Subtroch → plate on the lateral (tension) side → **tension band** (Nagah)
- Sagittal alignment → set by **rotating the plate on the screw** after insertion (MIPO)

### Indications · contraindications
| Use it | Avoid it |
|---|---|
| Subtroch, esp. involving both trochanters (Nagah) | <3–4 cm intact condyle (Campbell) |
| Lateral wall broken at the DHS entry (MIPO) | Articular comminution (Campbell) |
| Distal femur intercondylar fractures | Osteoporosis (Campbell) |

### Insertion
1) Reduce; Schanz screw as a joystick in the proximal fragment (MIPO)
2) Anteversion wire on the neck → **95° guide wire** parallel to it (MIPO)
3) **Triple reamer** → tap → **condylar screw**
4) Plate slid submuscularly, barrel over the screw → rotated to the shaft → cortical screws (MIPO)

### What goes wrong
- **Varus collapse and shortening** with medial comminution (Rockwood) · removes **much bone** → revision harder (Campbell)

- DCS fixing a subtrochanteric fracture in good alignment, X-ray (MIPO)

6.04.1.b:

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "angled blade plate"
- "**Angled blade plate**: a **U-profile blade** forged at a fixed angle to the plate, **95°** (condylar) or **130°**, driven into a track cut by a **seating chisel**."
- "**Fixed angle, no sliding**; today for **osteotomies, nonunions, malunions** and some subtroch fractures, and as a **reduction tool**."

### Recognise it · how it works
- **One piece**, no barrel, no head screw → the blade is the head fixation
- Blade gives **wider buttressing** (more contact area) than a condylar screw (Rockwood)
- Fixed angle → reducing the plate to the shaft **aligns the fracture** = "reduction plate"; no sliding → compress with a tension device (AO)

### Indications
- **Valgus osteotomy** (neck nonunion, malunion) → 120° or 130° blade for more valgus (AO)
- **Revision** of failed nail or DHS · subtroch with portal or lateral wall problems (Campbell)

### Insertion — three planes
1) Anteversion wire on the neck + 95° wire in the trochanter (MIPO)
2) **Seating chisel** with its guide → cut the track in all **three planes** (Campbell)
3) Remove the chisel → blade in with the **plate holder / impactor** (MIPO)
4) Reduce plate to shaft → eccentric screw → **articulated tension device** (Campbell)

- Seating chisel parallel to the joint line and the guide wire (AO)

- Wrong chisel track → **malalignment in any of three planes**; no percutaneous option (Campbell)
- Blade too posterior (distal femur) → condylar block shifts medially → **varus** (AO)

- Nonunion revised with a blade plate, head–trochanter relation restored (Rockwood)

6.06.b:
### Common frame for all of them
- Nail in the canal + **screw(s) or blade into head and neck** (Handbook) · trochanteric nails → **4–6° proximal bend** (Rockwood)
- Classes → impaction (blade: TFN = trochanteric fixation nail) · single lag screw (Gamma) · two screws (TriGen recon, Targon PFN) · integrated screws (InterTAN) (Rockwood)

- Five nail classes side by side (Rockwood)

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- Count the head elements → **Gamma 1 screw · PFNA 1 blade · PFN 2 unequal · recon 2 equal · InterTAN 2 integrated**

| Short nail | Long nail |
|---|---|
| Standard for most trochanteric fractures (Miller) | Reverse oblique, subtroch extension (Handbook) |
| Shorter operation, less blood loss (Campbell) | Pathological fracture, wide canal (Handbook) |
| Risk → fracture at the nail tip (AO) | Risk → **anterior cortex perforation** (Miller) |

#### Insertion — common steps
1) Fracture table; torso to the other side, hip adducted 10–15° (Handbook)
2) Reduce **before** reaming → no varus, no posterior sag, no excess internal rotation (Campbell)
3) Entry → **tip of the GT or just medial**; guide pin 2–3 cm deep (Campbell)
4) **Entry reamer** to below the lesser trochanter → ball-tip guide wire → measure length
5) Ream **1.5 mm over** the nail, 2 mm if bowed (Campbell)
6) Nail on the **jig**, guide anterior, rotate at halfway → depth for centre–centre (Campbell)
7) Sleeve through the jig → guide wire to 5 mm from subchondral bone → measure → ream → head element
8) Compress → distal locking, **static** (AO)

- Modified medial trochanteric portal (Campbell)

CLINICAL PEARL — four nail choices that prevent trouble
- **Diameter** → 10 mm for most; bigger → more anterior cortex perforation, no better outcome (Campbell)
- **Angle** → **130°**; a nail angle below the patient's neck–shaft angle → varus → cut-out (Campbell)
- **Long nail** → insert rotated **90°**, turn at halfway → less hoop stress, fewer GT fractures (Rockwood)
- **Short nail** → **static** distal locking → fewer shaft fractures than dynamic (Rockwood)

PITFALL — PFN entry point
- Nagah → **3 mm medial to the tip** of the greater trochanter
- Campbell / Rockwood → GT tip or the **medial trochanteric** portal, per nail design
- Say → "**tip of the trochanter or just medial; a lateral entry → varus**"

### PFN (Proximal Femoral Nail) — card

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "PFN"
- "**Proximal femoral nail**: trochanteric nail with **two parallel head screws of different sizes** → big lag screw below, small antirotation screw above."
- "Better rotational control; for **unstable trochanteric and subtrochanteric** fractures; typical failure → **Z-effect**."

- Recognise it → **two unequal screws** in the head, the smaller superior (AO)
- Sizes → lag screw **11 mm** below · antirotation hip pin **6.5 mm** above · nail 240 mm, proximal 17 mm (Jha 2020)
- How it works → load-sharing nail + sliding lag screw + antirotation hip screw
- **Z-effect** → upper screw into the joint while the lower backs out → high failure → **largely discontinued** (Rockwood)

- Z-effect on the X-ray (Rockwood)

### PFNA (Proximal Femoral Nail Antirotation) — card

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "PFNA"
- "**PFNA**: a trochanteric nail with **one helical blade** instead of two screws."
- "The blade is **hammered in, not screwed** → **compacts** cancellous bone → better hold and rotation control in **osteoporotic** bone; for unstable trochanteric and subtroch fractures."

- Recognise it → one **broad twisted blade** in the head · perforated → **cement augmentation** possible (AO)
- Larger bone contact → more cycles to failure (MIPO) · resists rotation better than one screw (Rockwood)
1) Common nail steps → guide wire centre–centre → drill the **lateral cortex only** (Rockwood)
2) **Impact** the blade, do not screw it → lock it to the nail (Rockwood)
3) Good bone → impaction may distract the fracture → blade is for **osteoporotic** bone (Rockwood)

- PFNA, perforated blade with cement augmentation, X-ray and CT (MIPO)
- PFNA with helical blade, 3D model (Zhang 2024)

PITFALL — TAD with a helical blade
- TAD <25 mm is for **lag screws**; blades migrate **medially** even with TAD <20 mm (Campbell)
- Helical blades → more fixation failure (odds ratio 1.88) than lag screws (Campbell)
- Say → "**blade: centre–centre, not too deep → or cut-through**"

### Gamma Nail — card

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "Gamma nail"
- "**Gamma nail**: shaped like the Greek **γ**, wide proximal nail with **one large sliding lag screw** → a sliding hip screw inside the canal."
- "For **trochanteric fractures**, stable or unstable; long version for subtrochanteric extension."

- Recognise it → **one thick lag screw** through a bulky proximal nail · proximal diameter **15.5–18 mm** (Rockwood)
- Third generation → **15.5 mm**, **4°** bend, GT-tip entry, tapered tip · first generation → shaft fractures up to **17%** (Rockwood)
- Gamma3 lag screw **10.5 mm** (was 12 mm) → smaller hole, stronger nail (Georgiannos 2014)
- Lag screw wire slightly below centre → ream → screw 5 mm shorter for compression → locking nut (Rockwood)

- Gamma nail insertion steps (Rockwood)

### InterTAN — card

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "InterTAN"
- "**InterTAN**: cephalomedullary nail with **two integrated screws** → lag screw + compression screw geared together → **linear compression**, resists rotation and cut-out."
- "**Trapezoidal** proximal section protects the lateral wall; for **unstable trochanteric** fractures."

- Recognise it → two screws **interlocked side by side**, trapezoidal proximal nail
- Proximal **16 mm**, 4° bend, **125° or 130°**, medial trochanteric entry (Rockwood)
- Screws push the nail to the **medial cortex** → unloads the lateral wall (Rockwood)

#### Insertion — its own steps (Rockwood)
1) Guide wire centre–centre to 5 mm from subchondral bone
2) Drill the **inferior** hole → **derotation bar** in
3) **10.5 mm** cannulated drill over the wire → **lag screw** 5–10 mm from subchondral bone
4) Bar out → **compression screw** in the inferior hole → release traction → compress

- InterTAN fixing a 31A3 fracture (Rockwood)
- InterTAN insertion steps (Rockwood)

6.10.b:
### TAD (tip–apex distance)
- **TAD** = lag screw tip to the head apex on **AP + lateral**, corrected for magnification (Baumgaertner 1995)
- None of **120 screws** with TAD ≤25 mm cut out, in 198 fractures (Baumgaertner 1995) · above 25 mm → risk rises **exponentially** (Campbell)
- Two-screw nails → centre–inferior position, TAD to the inferior screw (Rockwood)

- TAD on AP and lateral views, with the cut-out curve (Campbell)

PITFALL — TAD "> 25 mm" in Nagah
- Nagah writes TAD **> 25 mm** → wrong; AO, Campbell and Miller → **< 25 mm**
- Say → "**below 25 mm, centre–centre**"

### Cleveland zones
- Head divided into thirds on **AP** (superior–centre–inferior) and **lateral** (anterior–centre–posterior) → 9 zones
- **Centre–centre** protects; **centre–anterior** → ≈6 times the cut-out risk (Onder 2026) · inferior or posterior deviation acceptable (Handbook)

- Cleveland zones of the femoral head on AP and lateral views (Wittauer 2025; Thant 2026)

### Cut-out vs cut-through
| | Cut-out | Cut-through |
|---|---|---|
| What moves | head collapses into **varus**, screw breaks out **superiorly** | blade or screw migrates **medially** into the joint, no varus |
| Typical device | DHS, Gamma, PFN | PFNA / helical blades (Campbell) |
| Cause | eccentric superior screw, TAD >25 mm, osteoporosis (AO) | driven too deep, osteoporosis (Campbell) |
| Treatment | revision, arthroplasty, or accept in the non-ambulant (Nagah) | arthroplasty |

- Lag screw cut-out on a hip AP X-ray (Lingayat 2026)
- Helical blade cut-through into the hip joint, X-ray (Zhang 2023)

### Medialisation, Z-effect, varus collapse
- **Medialisation** → shaft slides medial; >1/3 shaft width → **7-fold** failure; from reverse oblique or a broken lateral wall (Rockwood)
- **Varus collapse** → neck–shaft angle lost → screw cuts out · **Z-effect** → two-screw nails → 6.6 · prevent both with a no-varus reduction (Campbell)

- Significant shortening (malunion) after screw–side plate fixation (Campbell)
- Varus malreduction of a subtrochanteric fracture ending in nonunion (Rockwood)

- **Centre** (Cleveland) · **Close** (TAD <25) · **Cortex** (lateral wall intact) · **Collapse** (medialisation, varus)

| What is this, its parts, its angles? | DHS: lag screw, barrel, side plate, compression screw · 130–150°, 135° standard |
| What is TAD? | lag screw tip to head apex, AP + lateral · keep **<25 mm** |
| Why the inverted triangle? | inferior on the calcar · two above against the cortices · parallel, peripheral |
| DHS in an unstable trochanteric fracture? ("why not a DHS here?") | reverse oblique, thin lateral wall → shaft medialises → nail, or DHS + TSP |
| Medialisation osteotomy to "make it stable"? | abandoned: no benefit, more blood loss (Rockwood) |
| Short vs standard barrel? | 22 + 20 + 38 = 80 mm · ≤80 mm → short barrel |
| Does the compression screw make it static? | no → compresses on the table, stops disengagement; sliding continues |
| Three ways to compress? | release traction · compression screw · weight bearing |
| Guide wire came out? | centring sleeve, or a reversed lag screw in the track |
| Coupling screws? | long → removal · short → inserting the lag screw into the plate |
